When creating a relation between entities of different services, we need to check if the referenced related entities managed by a different service are valid to use. Most importantly, does the given ID actually refer to an entity.
import related entities into service by listening to dapr creation events created by the owning service send a request to the owning service to verify that the entity with a given ID is valid

Chosen option: "import related entities into service by listening to dapr creation events created by the owning service", because results in more loose coupling, as we don't have synchronous requests between services when creating the relations. Note that there might be exceptions in cases where this approach is not applicable.

Good, because more loosely coupled: no requests sent when creating the relation, instead async notifications via the event bus when entities are created Neutral, because potentially more/less events/requests: reduces communication overhead when related entity is on average used more than once, otherwise increases overhead Bad, because less enforced consistency: e.g. deletion events might be delayed, can cause temporary inconsistencies (as usual with loose coupling)
documents.s: import related entities into service by listening to dapr creation events created by the owning service

documents.t: Good, because results in stricter consistency: always validates current state Neutral, because potentially more/less events/requests: reduces communication overhead when related entity is on average used less than once, otherwise increases overhead Bad, because results in tight coupling between services: relation to foreign entity can only be created if synchronous request to other service is successful
documents.s: send a request to the owning service to verify that the entity with a given ID is valid

documents.t: Category and product service are tightly coupled: The majority of endpoints of each services needs to either invoke the other service or duplicate the others services data: A product variant holds a characteristic value, this needs to be either saved in the product or category service. It is valuable to know if product variants with specific characteristic actually exist, when displaying the product categories in the frontend with each category characteristic. This prevents the user from running into empty queries. We only want to show characteristics to filter by, if product variants of the specific characteristic exists. Therefore the category service needs to know about the current product variants. Similarly, displaying a product variant includes its characteristic value, for example: size M for a t-shirt. Each product variant request depends on the characteristic value. A category can only be deleted if no product points to it. Should a category automatically be deleted if the last product referencing the category is deleted?

Save characteristic values of product variants in product service and let category service request the needed information Save characteristic values of product variants in category service and let product service request the needed information Data duplication in both services Merge category and product service Shared database (not up to discussion)
Chosen option: "Merge category and product service", because We do not see a clear cut that would still allow us to implement the functionality we want out of the system.
Good, querying products / product variants does not require querying the category service Bad, vice versa Bad, queries induce overhead
documents.s: Save characteristic values of product variants in product service and let category service request the needed information

documents.t: Good, filtering products / product variants for categories does not require querying the product service Bad, vice versa Bad, queries induce overhead
documents.s: Save characteristic values of product variants in category service and let product service request the needed information

documents.t: Bad, can lead to consistency problems Good, sync might create less overhead than just queries Bad, data duplications requires more memory
Bad, merging services reduces separation of concerns Good, prevents significant network overhead Neutral, one service less in total

APIs should support some kind of pagination when accessing a list of entities, to allow limiting API results to a managable size. In GraphQL, two approaches are popular: offset based pagination, where one specifies an offset in the list, and cursor based pagination, where a string serves as cursor to some element in the list.

cursor-based pagination (according to connection specification) with totalCount support cursor-based pagination (according to connection specification) without totalCount support offset-based pagination with totalCount support offset-based pagination without totalCount support
Chosen option: "offset-based pagination with totalCount support", because easier to implement, and we need totalCount support for the frontend.

A typical GraphQL schema will look like this: type Query { "Get a list of entities" entities( "Number of items to skip" skip: Int "Number of items to return" first: Int "Ordering" orderby: EntityOrder ): EntityConnection! } "A connection to a list of Entity values." type EntityConnection { "Whether this connection has a next page" hasNextPage: Boolean! "The resulting entities." nodes: [Entity!]! "The total amount of items in this connection" totalCount: Int! } "Entity order" input EntityOrderInput { "The field to order by" field: EntityOrderField "The direction to order by" direction: OrderDirection } "Order direction" enum OrderDirection { "Ascending order" ASC "Descending order" DESC } "Entity order fields" enum EntityOrderField { "Order entities by their id" ID } If the entity type of the connection is managed by a different service, knowledge of the entities is limited (typically only the id of the referenced entity is available). Thus, ordering support is limited to ID. To prevent conflicts between GraphQL type names, the following types MUST be used instead of EntityOrderInput: "Common order" input CommonOrderInput { "The field to order by" field: CommonOrderField "The direction to order by" direction: OrderDirection } "Common order fields" enum CommonOrderField { "Order entities by their id" ID }

Good, because hides away technical implementation (can be offset based or different) Good, because standardized: https://relay.dev/graphql/connections.htm Good, because includes totalCount support, allowing clients to display the amount of pages Bad, because difficult to implement: cursors have to encode values of all fields used in ordering Bad, because does not easily allow to start at an arbitrary offset
documents.s: cursor-based pagination (according to connection specification) with totalCount support

documents.t: Good, because hides away technical implementation (can be offset based or different) Good, because standardized: https://relay.dev/graphql/connections.htm Bad, because difficult to implement: cursors have to encode values of all fields used in ordering Bad, because does not easily allow to start at an arbitrary offset Bad, because clients cannot fetch the total amount of elements, which is necessary for some frontend designs
documents.s: cursor-based pagination (according to connection specification) without totalCount support

documents.t: Good, because allows to start at arbitrary offset Good, because easier to implement compared to cursor-based pagination (in particular with SQL databases) Good, because includes totalCount support, allowing clients to display the amount of pages Bad, because less flexible than cursor-based pagination Bad, because non-standard

Good, because allows to start at arbitrary offset Good, because easiest to implement (in particular with SQL databases), due to missing totalCount support Bad, because clients cannot fetch the total amount of elements, which is necessary for some frontend designs Bad, because less flexible than cursor-based pagination Bad, because non-standard

The buy process spans several services: an order has to reserve inventory, validate its discounts, be paid, be invoiced and be shipped. Each of these steps is a local transaction in a different service with its own database, so there is no shared transaction that could cover the whole process. We need to decide how the steps are coordinated, and what happens when one of them fails.

choreography: each service subscribes to the event concluding the previous step and publishes its own outcome, with compensation triggered by the service that detected the failure orchestration: a dedicated component drives the steps, tracks the state of the process and triggers compensation centrally retry failed steps indefinitely, and communicate only unrecoverable failures as events retry failed steps a bounded number of times, and treat exhaustion as an unrecoverable failure

Chosen options: "choreography" and "retry failed steps indefinitely, and communicate only unrecoverable failures as events", because they follow the loose coupling already established by ADR-6: we do not introduce a component that all participants depend on, and we do not need synchronous calls between the participating services. Two classes of error are assumed: transient errors, which are retried until they succeed, on the assumption that a temporarily unavailable service becomes available again after some time final failures, which are published as a dedicated event so that the affected services can undo their local work The resulting process is essentially linear, and it is documented in Order Saga and Failure Model.

Good, because no participant depends on a coordinator being available, and adding a step means subscribing to an existing event rather than changing a central definition. Good, because transient faults need no error handling in the participating services: the retry resolves them. Neutral, because the state of the process is not stored anywhere as a whole. In a linear saga the position in the process follows from the last event published. Bad, because the services are temporarily inconsistent with each other while the saga runs, and while a compensation propagates. Bad, because an error that is neither transient nor published as a final failure is retried for as long as it persists. Bad, because consumers can receive an event more than once, and therefore have to tolerate redelivery.

Good, because loosely coupled: no component that every participant depends on Good, because a new participant can join the process by subscribing to an event, without changing existing services Neutral, because the process is not described in one place: it follows from the events the services publish and subscribe to Bad, because no component holds the state of the process, so a step cannot wait for several predecessors without additional bookkeeping Bad, because whether every failure path is handled can only be determined by inspecting all participants

Good, because the process is defined in one place and its state is explicit, which makes parallel steps and joins straightforward Good, because compensation is decided centrally, based on the state of the whole process Bad, because every participant depends on the orchestrator Bad, because the orchestrator has to know about all participants, which couples it to each of them

Good, because simplest to implement: transient faults require no error handling in the services Good, because no step is abandoned while its dependency is merely unavailable Bad, because a persistent error that is not reported as a final failure keeps being retried Bad, because retries against an unavailable or saturated service add load to it
documents.s: retry failed steps indefinitely, and communicate only unrecoverable failures as events

documents.t: Good, because every step reaches a defined outcome, including errors that were not anticipated Neutral, because it requires deciding a bound, and a bound that is too low turns an ordinary outage into a failed order Bad, because it requires a place to put the events whose retries were exhausted, and a way to handle them
documents.s: retry failed steps a bounded number of times, and treat exhaustion as an unrecoverable failure

documents.t: The frontend needs to be able to send requests to the backend. As such requests need to be instrumented with tracing metadata, and authentication needs to be performed, an API gateway should be provided. However, different API technologies exist, and we need to decide which one to use
GraphQL REST gRPC Web
Chosen option: "GraphQL", because allows frontend to use one unified API to fetch data from the backend

Good, because allows frontend to easily fetch and combine data from different sources in the backend Neutral, because requires us to find a way how to combine API of different services into one unified GraphQL API

Good, because allows frontend to easily fetch and combine data from different sources in the backend Good, because built-in strict type system Good, because GraphiQL allows users to explore the API, including with a graphical interface to build requests Good, because allows client to define which data should be fetched, reducing overfetching Good, because allows to solve N+1 problem of requests, as instead of multiple consecutive requests, a single request can define all data which needs to be fetched Bad, because more difficult to implement, in particular regarding authorization

Good, because easiest to implement, in particular regarding authentication Good, because easy to use for users of the reference architecture Good, because good for browser caching Neutral, because no built-in typing, but could be provided via OpenAPI Bad, because more difficult to combine data from different sources: combine in gateway? have all routes from services in gateway? Bad, because does not allow frontend to define which data should be fetched

Good, because allows streaming Good, because built-in type system Good, because binary protocol is more efficient Neutral, because binary format is more difficult to understand in web environment, in particular form users of the reference architecture, but text-based protocol could also be used. JSON could also be used, but it is non-standard. Bad, because less common in web environments compared to other options Bad, because compared to GraphQL, does not provide unified way for client to define which data should be fetched
We consider two different ways of building our frontend: either a micro frontend, or a monolithic frontend.
micro frontend monolithic frontend

Chosen option: "monolithic frontend", because with the given resources (5 developers) and experiences, a monolithic frontend is easier to implement and thus allows us to focus on more important aspects of the reference architecture

Good, because we do not need to consider requirements of a micro frontend with respect to the API gateway Neutral, because there is a single repository for the frontend. Good, because the frontend tech stack can be chosen rather freely. We decided to use Vue with Vuetify to create a single page web application. Neutral, because all services have to support the API gateway for the frontend.

Good, because would result in our whole stack to be "micro" from end-to-end Good, because would frontends of services to be developed independently Bad, because more difficult to implement, in particular with regard to given resources Bad, because there are several frontend components, which are not clearly associated with a specific backend service

Good, because easier to implement, thus allowing us to focus on more important aspects of the reference architecture Good, because simplifies defining frontend components independant of backend service structure Bad, because results in whole stack not being "micro" end-to-end

documents.s: Design Choices in the Domain Model

documents.t: The domain model does not automatically add returned items back to the Inventory. They need to be added manually, similar to a shipment from the manufacturer, or thrown away.

A User cannot reserve items by putting them in the ShoppingCart: The Inventory contains ProductItems as instances of a ProductVariant. These ProductItems do not know about existing ShoppingCarts or ShoppingCartItems. Thus, when the user wants to finish the order, the system must check whether the ProductItem is still in stock, since it could have been ordered by another user in the meantime. A User can have exactly one ShoppingCart at a time, independent of the client device used.

An Invoice is associated with exactly one Order. Split invoices for parts of the order are not supported. A Payment is only created after the associated Invoice has been paid. The store supports only payment methods where the payment is completed before the shipping of any ordered items.

A Coupon is a promotional offer. It allows a User to apply a Discount to a Product. Each Coupon is associated with a specific Discount. The store only offers Discounts in percentages. The store does not have gift cards. The Discount can have whitelist filters by Product, ProductVariant, and Category. If filters are present, the Discount can be applied to Products matching any filter. If no filters are present, the Discount can be applied to all products.

Each ProductVariantVersion has its TaxRate specified. Thus, the store cannot easily operate in multiple tax rate regions. Tax deduction for business accounts are not supported by the system, since the TaxRate is fixed for all Users.

A Notification is within-the-system; they are not forwarded to emails, text messages, or anything else. Notifications are read-only. Users can only receive notifications, they cannot reply to them. Each Notification is sent to exactly one user. There are no broadcasts.

To be able to order something from the store, a User needs an Account. This implies that the store does not support something like "checkout as guest". Addresses stored by the system do not have to be unique physical addresses. The system may store multiple instances of the same physical address. One Address cannot be related to multiple User instances. A user's Wishlists are private and cannot be seen by other users.
documents.s: How Users relate to their Account, Wishlists, and Addresses

documents.t: The store has no Category hierarchy.
The buy process spans several services. This page describes how their work is coordinated at runtime, and how failures are handled.

Coordination is purely event-based. There is no orchestrator component, and no service drives the process centrally. Each participant subscribes to the event that concludes the preceding step, performs a local transaction, and publishes the outcome as a new event. The events are exchanged via dapr pub/sub as described in the component diagram. The saga is essentially linear. The steps form a chain rather than a graph, and no step waits for several predecessors to complete. Only two events have more than one subscriber, and in both cases the additional subscriber performs work that the rest of the chain does not depend on.

Step Triggered by Service Action Publishes 1 Order is placed Order Records the order with status PLACED order/order/created 2 order/order/created Inventory Reserves the ProductItems for the order inventory/product-item/reservation-succeeded or reservation-failed 3 inventory/product-item/reservation-succeeded Discount Validates the order to check if the discounts can still be applied discount/order/validation-succeeded or validation-failed 4 discount/order/validation-succeeded Payment Starts the payment process payment/payment/payment-enabled, then payment-processed or payment-failed 5 payment/payment/payment-enabled Shipment Creates the shipments for the order shipment/shipment/created or creation-failed 6 shipment/shipment/created, shipment/shipment/status-updated Inventory Updates the inventory status based on the shipment status -- Two steps have a second subscriber alongside the one that continues the chain: On discount/order/validation-succeeded, the Invoice service creates the invoice and publishes invoice/invoice/created. On payment/payment/payment-enabled, the Inventory service sends the reserved inventory to fulfillment. The ShoppingCart service also subscribes to order/order/created to remove the ordered items from the cart, and the Return service imports the Order and later the Shipment so that returns can reference them. Neither is part of the buy saga itself.
The saga distinguishes two classes of error.

Errors that are expected to resolve on their own are handled by retrying. Most processes retry indefinitely. The underlying assumption is that a service which is temporarily unavailable becomes available again after some time, so the step eventually succeeds without intervention. Transient errors are therefore not represented as events, and they do not abort the saga.

Errors that will not resolve by retrying are communicated explicitly, as a dedicated event. There is no central coordinator that detects them or decides what to do: the service that detects the failure publishes the corresponding failure event, and each affected participant reacts by undoing its own local work. Detected by Failure event Reacting service Compensating action Discount discount/order/validation-failed Inventory Releases the product items related to the order Payment payment/payment/payment-failed Inventory Releases the product items related to the order Shipment shipment/shipment/creation-failed Order Triggers order compensation and publishes order/order-compensation/created

Because each step commits locally and the outcome travels as an event, the participating services are not consistent with each other for the duration of the saga, and in particular while a compensation is still propagating. This is an accepted consequence of the loosely coupled, event-based coordination chosen in ADR-6 and ADR-7.

Besides the various views to interact with the system, there are two important components in the frontend: The Pinia store and the GraphQL client.

The role of the Pinia Store in Vue is to manage the state of the application in a centralized and reactive manner, facilitating state manipulation and sharing across components. The store manages: login state the active user role the user's shopping cart the notification queue

The GraphQL client is the interface to the backend services. All communication with the backend is done through the GraphQL client. It provides functions for sending queries and mutations to the backend and receiving responses.

The gateway is the entry point for the MisArch system. It is responsible for routing requests to the correct service and handling authentication. Requests are forwarded via dapr service invocation to the respective service.

The media service provides the bounded context Media. It is responsible for managing media files such as images. The media services uses a Nginx reverse proxy to make the fixed domain of MinIO pre-signed URLs configurable through environment variables. A pre-signed URL is used as a reference to a specific media. It is generated for each Media entity when the path attribute is requested. This is necessary for access control to specific media files. A Media entity cannot be queried by a user client directly. It is used in within the service mesh by other services to reference medias in the services datatypes. Pre-signed URLs link media to authenticated service datatypes, chaining authentication. Each request of the path attribute on Media generates a new pre-signed URL with a limited validity duration. In other words, presigned URLS are generated automatically without any interference and attachments will always vanish once the presigned URL is no longer valid The service parses the following environment variables: MINIO_ENDPOINT: configurable domain of the MinIO instance. PATH_EXPIRATION_TIME: validity duration of MinIO pre-signed URLs in seconds. A resource can no longer be reached under the pre-signed URL after the pre-signed URL is expired. PROXY_PATH: path to include in the pre-signed URLs.

In the following, the most important business processes are modeled using BPMN. note These models describe the intended business processes, not the way the services coordinate them at runtime. The buy process below shows its steps in parallel with a joining gateway, and compensation handled centrally. The implementation is event-based and essentially linear, and compensation is triggered by the service that detected the failure. See Order Saga and Failure Model for how the buy process is actually coordinated.

The system needs a way to manage and authenticate users. There are two kinds of users: regular users (customers) and employees with extra permissions. FR-1.1: Users can authenticate to the shop ("login"). FR-1.2: Visitors can browse products, categories, and search results without logging in. FR-1.3: Product Management functions are restricted to authenticated employees.
The system needs to support the management of products, as well as discovery and browsing of the product by users.

Employee users can create, edit, and delete products. Products can have variants that alter certain attributes of the product, such as its color. FR-2.1: Employees can create new products or edit existing ones. FR-2.2: Employees can add, edit, or delete variants of a product. FR-2.3: Each variant can have at least a name, description, and product images. FR-2.4: A variant can be "default", which means it will be the default variant for users when they view the product. FR-2.5: Products can be grouped in product categories. Each category can have characteristics that apply to all products in the category, such as "color" or "size". FR-2.6: A Product can belong to multiple categories. FR-2.6: A product and variant needs to be set to "visible" to appear to non-employee users. FR-2.7: Each variant must have a retail price, and can have a (lower) selling price if the product is on a sale.

A visitor or regular user wants to find the products they need. They can do this by browsing the homepage, navigating through categories, or using a text search function. FR-2.8: Users and visitors can browse products from the homepage. FR-2.9: Users and visitors can see and navigate product categories. FR-2.10: Users and visitors can search for products using a text-based search function. FR-2.11: Within product categories or search results, users and visitors can apply filters.

When a user has found a product they are interested in, they want to inspect the product details, such as its description, variants, and reviews. FR-2.12: Users and visitors can open a product detail page. FR-2.13: The product detail page should contain the product details, including its description, available variants, and customer reviews.

Once the user has found the products they want to buy, they need a way to purchase them. The system needs to support a shopping cart and a checkout process. FR-3.1: Users can add products or variants to a shopping cart. FR-3.2: Users can view the contents of their shopping cart. FR-3.3: Users can change the quantity of items in their shopping cart or remove them from the shopping cart. FR-3.5: The system shall support the checkout process as detailed on the Business Processes page.

After the user has placed an order as part of the checkout, they want to keep track of their orders. If they are not satisfied, they might want to return an item. FR-4.1: Users can access to their order history. FR-4.2: Users can view details of their orders. FR-4.3: Users can see the current status of their orders. FR-4.4: Users can return process products as detailed on the Business Processes page. FR-4.5: Users can download invoices for each order. Each invoice includes the order details, the total price, and the tax information.

Sometimes, a user does not want to buy a product right away, but wants to save it on a wishlist. FR-5.1: Each user can have multiple wishlists. FR-5.2: A user can create, edit, and delete wishlists. FR-5.3: Each wishlist has a name. FR-5.4: Products can be added to wishlists from the product details page.

To increase customer trust and provide feedback to the store, users can submit reviews for products they have purchased. FR-6.1: Authenticated users can submit product reviews for products they have purchased. FR-6.2: Each review has a title, rating, and text content. FR-6.3: Users can create reviews directly from a product page, or from the order history. FR-6.4: Reviews are published immediately upon submission.

The shop operator wants to incentivize orders by offering promotions, such as discounts. FR-7.1: The shop operator can create discounts that apply a percentage off a product's price. FR-7.2: A discount has a validity period, and can have a minimum order amount, maximum number of uses, and a maximum discount amount, all set by the shop operator. FR-7.3: A discount can be applied with a coupon-code. FR-7.4: A discount can be scoped to a number of products or product variants, and is not generally usable.

Non-functional requirements (NFRs) specify the quality attributes and constraints that the system must satisfy. These requirements are derived from business goals and operational needs rather than specific features.

Fast response times improve user experience, increase conversion rates, and reduce cart abandonment. Response times are critical during promotional events when user engagement is highest. NFR-1.1: Product search, browsing, and category navigation shall complete within 500-800ms on average. Occasional delays up to 2-3 seconds are acceptable for power users during high-load periods. NFR-1.2: Adding items to cart and checkout operations shall complete within 1 second on average to minimize user frustration at critical transaction points. NFR-1.3: Product detail page loading (including images, descriptions, reviews, and variants) shall complete within 1 second on average. NFR-1.4: Initial page load for the homepage and category pages shall complete within 2 seconds including all static assets.

The system must be available during peak shopping times, especially during promotional events, to maximize revenue and customer satisfaction. E-commerce platforms lose revenue during outages. Promotional events are high-profit periods, making availability during these times critical. Graceful degradation ensures users can continue shopping even when some features are unavailable. NFR-2.1: The system shall achieve 99%+ uptime during business hours (06:00 - 23:59 daily). Downtime during off-peak hours (02:00 - 06:00) has lower priority. NFR-2.2: The system shall handle promotional events and flash sales without outages or degraded performance, even with significant traffic spikes (estimated 5-10x normal load). NFR-2.3: The system shall automatically recover from temporary failures (e.g., database connection timeouts, service crashes) within 2-5 minutes without manual intervention. NFR-2.4: If a service becomes unavailable, the system shall gracefully degrade by either serving cached data, showing appropriate error messages, or disabling specific features rather than failing completely. Especially critical functions (product browsing, searching, adding to cart, checkout, payment processing) should remain operational when non-critical services (reviews, wishlists, user profiles) experience temporary issues.
documents.s: 2. Availability & Reliability - High System Availability During Business Hours

documents.t: Users and the business must trust that orders, payments, and inventory updates are processed correctly and consistently. Incorrect orders, duplicate charges, or lost inventory information damage reputation and revenue. NFR-3.1: All orders placed by users shall be recorded exactly once in the system. Lost orders are unacceptable. Duplicate orders need to be prevented or detected and resolved automatically. NFR-3.2: Inventory updates (after an order is placed) shall be reflected consistently across the system within 10 minutes at maximum. Overbooking products should be prevented, thus inventory updates shall be updated in the checkout process within 30 seconds to avoid overselling. NFR-3.3: Payment transactions shall be atomic: either an order is fully confirmed with payment, or the transaction is completely rolled back. Partial order states are unacceptable. NFR-3.4: User shopping carts and wishlist contents shall remain consistent and not be lost during system failures or deploys.
documents.s: 3. Data Integrity & Consistency - Reliable Order Processing

documents.t: The system must comply with data protection regulations and protect sensitive customer information. Data breaches result in regulatory fines, customer trust loss, and reputational damage. Compliance is mandatory in EU markets. NFR-4.1: The system shall comply with GDPR and EU data protection regulations, including user consent management, data subject rights (access, deletion, portability), and data breach notification procedures. NFR-4.2: All payment information (credit card numbers, bank details) shall be processed securely via PCI-DSS compliant payment gateways. The system shall never store raw payment card data. NFR-4.3: User authentication shall use strong, industry-standard methods (e.g., bcrypt, Argon2) to hash passwords. Passwords shall never be transmitted or logged in plain text. NFR-4.4: All communication between users and the system, and between internal services, shall use encrypted channels (HTTPS/TLS). NFR-4.5: User data (addresses, order history, reviews) shall be protected from unauthorized access. Access to sensitive data shall be logged and auditable. NFR-4.6: The system shall have clear data retention policies and automatically delete personal data when no longer needed (e.g., after user account deletion or after a retention period).
documents.s: 4. Security & Data Privacy - Protect User Data and Payment Information

documents.t: The system must accommodate increased traffic, data volume, and concurrent users without requiring rewrites or extended downtime. The system should be able to handle slow, sustained business growth. NFR-5.1: The system shall support 10x increase in concurrent users and transactions through horizontal scaling (adding more servers) rather than requiring hardware upgrades or architectural changes. NFR-5.2: The system shall automatically scale up resources during traffic spikes (e.g., promotional events) and scale down during low-traffic periods to optimize costs. NFR-5.3: The system architecture shall allow independent scaling of different services. For example, if product browsing is slow, that service can be scaled without scaling payment processing. NFR-5.4: The system shall remain responsive and reliable with future business growth. A slow, sustained increase in users should not cause problems with appropriate handling in operations, and should not cause a need for big refactorings or rewrites.
documents.s: 5. Scalability - Handling User Spikes and Business Growth

documents.t: Operations and development teams must be able to monitor, debug, and improve the system in production. Microservices add operational complexity. Without good observability, debugging is time-consuming and expensive. Poor observability increases mean-time-to-recovery during incidents. NFR-6.1: The system shall provide comprehensive logging for all significant operations (user actions, service calls, errors, transactions). Logs shall be centralized and searchable. NFR-6.2: The system shall expose detailed metrics (response times, error rates, resource usage) that are collected automatically and visualized in dashboards. Teams shall be able to identify bottlenecks and anomalies. NFR-6.3: The system shall enable distributed request tracing across microservices. When a user complains about slow checkout, teams shall be able to see which service was the bottleneck. NFR-6.4: System errors shall include sufficient context for debugging (stack traces, relevant state, request details) without exposing sensitive data to end users. NFR-6.5: Teams shall be able to deploy new versions without downtime or customer impact (e.g., via blue-green deployments or gradual rollouts). NFR-6.6: The system shall automatically detect an increase of slow responses, both in case of a small increase for a long time and a sudden spike.
documents.s: 6. Maintainability & Observability - Understand and Troubleshoot the System
